query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small interstitial concentration of carbon (around 0.3–0.5 at.%) into equiatomic NbMoTaW will activate additional deformation mechanisms—specifically, twinning and transformation‐induced plasticity—that improve room‐temperature ductility without reducing its high-temperature yield strength or its intrinsic irradiation tolerance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, equimolar NbMoTaW with a BCC structure that exhibits excellent high-temperature (≈1600 °C) mechanical performance but very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-level (≈0.3–0.5 at.%) addition of interstitial carbon during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Assess under room temperature tensile/compressive deformation, high-temperature mechanical testing at 1600 °C, and irradiation exposure (e.g., up to several dpa with ion irradiations) under standardized testing protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: The carbon atoms are expected to segregate within the BCC matrix to form coherent nano-sized features (or induce slight local ordering) that serve as nucleation sites for deformation twins and/or trigger localized phase transformation (TWIP/TRIP effects) without forming a continuous carbide network.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon lowers the barrier for dislocation mobility and promotes the activation of multiple plasticity mechanisms – like nano-twinning (TWIP) and localized phase transformation (TRIP) – which delay strain localization and enhance ductility at room temperature. Since the carbon content is kept very low, it is not expected to disrupt the high-melting BCC matrix that controls the excellent strength at 1600 °C, nor does it significantly alter defect migration energies that underpin irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit a substantial increase in room-temperature ductility (higher strain-to-failure and improved work hardening) while retaining similar high-temperature yield strength. Under irradiation, the defect tolerance should remain at least as good as the undoped alloy, with minimal irradiation hardening or phase instabilities.
generation.baseline: Untreated equimolar NbMoTaW, which is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature strength and predicted irradiation resistance but extremely limited room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects rely on keeping the carbon content very low (ideally <0.5 at.%) to avoid excessive carbide formation or the emergence of brittle secondary phases, which could compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation tolerance. The processing must ensure homogeneous interstitial distribution without segregation at grain boundaries that might otherwise embrittle the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the demonstration that interstitial atoms can activate TWIP/TRIP mechanisms in other HEA systems (e.g., evidence in PMC5227964) and on reports that trace dopants such as carbon can improve grain-boundary strength in refractory HEAs (as noted in literature akin to the findings mentioned in PMC9586648). However, the exact behavior of interstitial carbon in a strictly equiatomic NbMoTaW system, particularly regarding long‐term irradiation effects and high-temperature stability, remains unverified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples under identical processing conditions – one set with no carbon addition (the control) and one set with a defined interstitial addition of approximately 0.3–0.5 at.% carbon. Perform mechanical testing at room temperature (e.g., tensile/compressive tests to measure ductility and work hardening behavior), high-temperature testing at around 1600 °C (to verify yield strength retention), and controlled irradiation experiments (using ion irradiations to a predetermined dpa level) with accompanying microstructural characterization (via TEM, atom probe tomography, etc.).
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strain-to-failure and work hardening rate
Irradiation-induced microstructural evolution and hardness changes pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped NbMoTaW samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the undoped control, or if they exhibit a reduction in high-temperature strength or degradation of irradiation resistance (e.g., formation of detrimental carbides or increased irradiation hardening), then the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

These improvements in mechanical properties of the iHEA compared to substitutional HEAs are due to the multiple strengthening mechanisms active in the new material. The EBSD phase maps (Fig. 4a) show that the metastable f.c.c phase in the iHEA undergoes a strain-induced martensitic transformation from the f.c.c to the h.c.p phase as a primary deformation mechanism affecting the entire bulk matrix. The fraction of transformed h.c.p. phase at the necking stage (εloc = 90%) is 36.5% (in area%), which is much lower than that observed for the substitutional TRIP-DP-HEAs (area% >75%),. This observation shows that the f.c.c. phase in the iHEA has a higher stability than in the TRIP-DP-HEA. After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
